items.text:
This passage is the payoff of the essay's fourth and final argument against "computational functionalism" — the assumption, named back in [spya-wepmnr], that running the right computation is enough, by itself, to produce consciousness. Having spent three sections arguing that brains aren't really computers, that other non-computational dynamics may matter, and that life itself may be a necessary ingredient, Seth now attacks the fallback position: even if none of that convinces you, surely a *sufficiently detailed simulation* of a brain would still produce consciousness? This block is where he says no.

The move is a distinction between simulating something and instantiating it. Computational simulations generally lack the causal powers and intrinsic properties of the things being simulated. A simulation of the digestive system does not actually digest anything. A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet. The general principle he draws from these examples is stated right in this block: a computational simulation of X does not bring X into being — does not instantiate X — unless X is a computational process (specifically, an algorithm) itself. Making the point from the other direction, the fact that X can be simulated computationally does not justify the conclusion that X is itself computational.

Worth knowing, as background the article doesn't spell out: this "simulated storm doesn't make you wet" style of example is closely associated with the philosopher John Searle, whose biological naturalism Seth invokes earlier in the essay [spya-hj5y6s] and who is famous for a similar argument (the "Chinese Room") that formal symbol-manipulation alone can't produce understanding. Seth is working in that same lineage, though he doesn't name Searle at this specific point — only two blocks earlier, in a different context.

The reason this block matters for what follows: it sets up the next paragraph's conclusion, where Seth applies the principle directly to consciousness — A computational simulation of the brain (and body), however detailed it may be, will only give rise to consciousness if consciousness is a matter of computation. In other words, the prospect of instantiating consciousness through some kind of whole-brain emulation, at some arbitrarily high level of detail, already assumes that computational functionalism is true. That's the target he's really aiming at: the popular dream of mind-uploading, which he goes on to puncture a few paragraphs later by comparing an uploaded "you" to a hailstorm inside a weather-forecasting computer [spya-xvm37k]. So this passage is best read as a hinge — the abstract principle (simulation ≠ instantiation) that the following paragraphs cash out against a very concrete fantasy (digital immortality).
items.context: Computational simulations generally lack the causal powers and intrinsic properties of the things being simulated. A simulation of the digestive system does not actually digest anything. A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet. If we simulate a living creature, we have not created life. In general, a computational simulation of X does not bring X into being — does not instantiate X — unless X is a computational process (specifically, an algorithm) itself. Making the point from the other direction, the fact that X can be simulated computationally does not justify the conclusion that X is itself computational.

items.text:
This passage is the emotional and argumentative peak of Seth's third argument against conscious AI — the claim that "life (probably) matters" for consciousness [spya-hj5y6s]. It's pushing the idea introduced a few paragraphs earlier as far down as it will go: not just to whole brains or bodies, but into every single cell.

To follow it, you need two pieces of vocabulary the passage assumes you're carrying from earlier in this same section:

**"Prediction error minimization"** is the technical name for the theory Seth sketched a few blocks up: the brain doesn't passively receive the world, it constantly guesses what's out there and adjusts based on the mismatch ("prediction error") between guess and incoming signal [spya-dp8sem]. He calls conscious experience itself a "controlled hallucination" built this way [spya-xhvztm], and extends the same logic to bodily feelings like emotion and mood via "interoceptive inference" — best-guessing about the body's internal state [spya-hzp9yz spya-b59nm2].

**"Autopoietic"** was defined earlier, in the "Brains Are Not Computers" section: it's the Greek-derived term (self-production) for how living things — down to a single neuron — spend their existence maintaining and regenerating their own physical basis, rather than just processing inputs [spya-cf8rt8]. Seth flags it there as arguably the defining mark of being alive, as opposed to being a computer.

What this passage does is fuse those two ideas. "This drive to stay alive doesn't bottom out anywhere in particular" means the self-preserving, predicting activity isn't something that only happens at the level of a brain regulating a whole body — it goes all the way down into "the molecular furnaces of metabolism," i.e. the chemical work inside individual cells [spya-vys3vj]. The claim is that the same predictive, error-minimizing process that (on his account) underlies conscious experience is, at bottom, indistinguishable from the basic chemistry of staying alive — hence "inseparable from the materiality of life itself" [spya-vys3vj].

The next paragraph then cashes this out as the argument's payoff: he says the connection between life and consciousness starts to come into view precisely because both phenomena bottom out in the same biological, non-computational processes [spya-da9tvt]. So this passage is the hinge — the point where "prediction error minimization" (a cognitive-science idea) and "autopoiesis" (a biological idea) are claimed to be, at the cellular level, one and the same thing. If you didn't have autopoiesis and prediction-error-minimization already defined in your head from the earlier blocks, this paragraph would read as a mystical flourish rather than what it's meant to be: the load-bearing joint of his "life matters" argument.

Worth noting, though not something the article spells out: outside this piece, autopoiesis is a term coined by the biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela in the 1970s, which is worth knowing if you want to chase the idea further than Seth does here.
items.context: This drive to stay alive doesn’t bottom out anywhere in particular. It reaches deep into the interior of each cell, into the molecular furnaces of metabolism. Within these whirls of metabolic activity, the ubiquitous process of prediction error minimization becomes inseparable from the materiality of life itself. A mathematical line can be drawn directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self.
